title_en: Indian man jailed over US murder plot against Sikh separatist
content_en:
Nikhil Gupta received a sentence of more than 19 years in prison for orchestrating the failed assassination plan in New York.
Nikhil Gupta stands beside his lawyer, Isabelle Kirshner, as he is sentenced by US District Judge Victor Marrero in New York on Friday. Courtroom sketch: Jane Rosenberg via Reuters
An Indian man was sentenced to more than 19 years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to ‌kill a Sikh separatist in New York, in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
US District Judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a hearing in Manhattan federal court.
The discovery of alleged assassination ⁠plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India, which has denied involvement ‌in such plots.
Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice ‌in New York, who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.
Gupta ⁠and the Indian government ⁠official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have US$15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who was actually an undercover US law enforcement ‌officer, court papers show.
Gurpatwant Singh Pannun speaks during the sentencing of Nikhil Gupta in New York on Friday. Courtroom sketch: Jane Rosenberg via Reuters
Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired ‌a defence ‌lawyer.
India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government ‌policy.
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.
“This ⁠case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone ⁠the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”
Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the nonviolent example set by Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.
“I’m ‌sorry to Mr Pannun, ‌I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta said.
Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.
“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.
By Reuters

title_en: Trump says China agreed to trilateral despite reluctance, notes nuclear gap
content_en:
US president cited Beijing’s wariness was due to difference between their arsenal and the much larger stockpiles held by America and Russia.
US President Donald Trump speaks at a  White House news conference in Washington on Friday. Photo: AP
US President Donald Trump said on Friday that China had agreed to hold trilateral nuclear risk-reduction talks for the first time despite earlier reluctance, as he acknowledged the wide gap between Beijing’s arsenal and the much larger stockpiles held by the US and Russia.
“They didn’t want to do that because China ... is way behind,” Trump said in a press conference at the White House.
“We have estimates of 4,000 nuclear weapons. Russia’s second to us, and China’s way behind. But they’ll catch us within 10 years.”
The United States and Russia held total inventories of 5,042 and 5,420 nuclear warheads, respectively, as of January, compared with an estimated 620 for China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
His remarks come a day after he attended a historic trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.
[embedded media]
The leaders of the world’s major nuclear powers released a joint statement pledging dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, commitments to reform the United Nations, plans to boost refined petroleum supplies and warnings against international courts.
“The three heads of state reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” the statement said.
“The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”
Leaders’ joint statement focused on nuclear risk reduction
The South China Morning Post earlier reported that the joint statement would focus on nuclear risk reduction and include the specific pledge against nuclear war.
During the meeting, Xi said that “nuclear weapons, the Sword of Damocles that hangs over humanity, should be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons”.
He also laid out a four-point framework for how China, Russia and the US should manage ties, urging them to act as “partners and friends”, avoid conflict and confrontation, maintain peaceful coexistence and overcome the Thucydides Trap – the risk of war when a rising power challenges an established hegemony.
He added that China, Russia and the US should “put themselves in each other’s shoes and act prudently on major sensitive issues involving one another – and in particular, avoid crossing each other’s red lines.”
Trump echoed the sentiment, saying: “We have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people but the entire planet.”
In a statement on Friday following Trump’s four-day visit to the Philippines and China, the White House also highlighted his first-ever trilateral summit with Xi and Putin.
“President Trump will meet with anyone who is willing to work together to make the lives of Americans – and the world – more prosperous and secure,” it said, adding that he called for nuclear weapons reductions and an end to the Ukraine war.
The statement also touted over US$17 billion in deals, a trade agreement with Thailand and meetings with Quad and Asean leaders in the Philippines.
Earlier on Thursday, Trump held his third bilateral meeting of the year with the Chinese leader, following his May visit to Beijing and Xi’s September trip to the US.
Xi reiterated that the two countries had agreed to build a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability and added new substance to it by placing the relationship on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to a readout released by China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Xi added that the “overall stability” of bilateral ties had brought tangible benefits to both nations and he looked forward to working with Trump to keep “this giant ship” on the right course and “forge ahead at full sail”.
[embedded media]
On Taiwan, Xi said that the “US side should keep doing the right thing and avoid major setbacks in China-US relations”.
The White House did not release a separate readout of the bilateral meeting.
Greer says Beijing raised Taiwan issue during talks
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Friday that the Chinese side raised the Taiwan issue during the talks, but it’s not a “point of contention” between the two sides.
“The Chinese have their views on Taiwan and independence. We have our one-China policy we’ve had for decades that hasn’t changed,” Greer said in an interview with Bloomberg.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.
On rare earths and discussions on extending the Busan agreement, Greer said the issue was “addressed” in the Trump-Xi bilateral and that Xi “himself acknowledged that this is something where they want to make sure that they are responsive to US requests”.
“The Chinese, of course, have their own requests of us, and so we’re trying between the two of us to maintain this Busan agreement, this Busan accord, where we can have stability in these discrete areas, rare earths, tariff levels, etc …” he added.
“We are in full compliance with Busan. We expect the Chinese to fully comply as well.”
The deal reached in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, helped ease bilateral tensions that had surged following Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs.
Under the pact, Washington agreed to cut tariffs on certain Chinese imports and shelve further trade restrictions. Beijing, in turn, paused some rare earth export controls and pledged to purchase US soybeans and curb exports of chemicals used to make fentanyl.
The US has repeatedly pressed Beijing to increase rare earth shipments, linking the flows to the extension of the Busan agreement. The agreement was extended by just two months in September and faces a January 10, 2027, deadline.
By Nayan Seth

title_en: Denmark expels Russian diplomat over plot to kill Ukraine rapper
content_en:
The country is also considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians.
The head of the Danish national security and intelligence service, PET, Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen (left) and Danish National Police Chief Lasse Boje Nielsen speak to the media about a suspected attempted assassination of a Ukrainian rapper in Soeborg, near Copenhagen, on Friday. Photo: AFP
Denmark’s foreign minister on Friday said Moscow’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Russia was suspected of being behind an attempted assassination of a Ukrainian rapper.
“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark” within seven days, Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference.
He also added Denmark was mulling suspending Schengen visas for the European border-free area to Russian nationals.
Reacting to the announcement afterwards, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called it “a clear illustration of the serious security situation in which Denmark and Europe find themselves”.
“We are facing a cornered Russia, acting more aggressively and with a greater propensity to take risks,” she said, quoted in a statement.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen talks to journalists in Copenhagen on Thursday. Photo: Reuters
Earlier in the day, the Danish PET intelligence agency said it suspected Russia of planning the assassination of a Ukrainian rapper during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb with the help of a Danish criminal gang banned since 2021.
According to the PET, three people were intercepted in a car nearby just before the concert. A search of the vehicle found firearms and knives.
Two people were placed under formal investigation on Friday for attempted murder and for assisting a foreign intelligence service in its operations within Denmark.
Police and the intelligence services suspect Loyal to Familia, a Danish street gang and criminal network, of having taken part in the planning of the hit.
“The case shows, in our assessment, that the Russian intelligence services attempted to carry out an execution in Denmark,” the head of PET, Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, said at a press conference.
Denmark’s public television DR identified the rapper as Kyivstoner, who holds both Ukrainian and American citizenship.
Since Russia’s invasion nearly five years ago, Denmark has been a key supporter of Ukraine.
“The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine. And we fully intend to continue,” Rasmussen said.
“Moscow will give an appropriate response,” Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said, as quoted by TASS news agency.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Anthropic researcher says Claude AI has solved maths’ greatest riddle: Riemann Hypothesis
content_en:
The Riemann Hypothesis, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, has stumped mathematicians for more than 160 years.
Levent Alpoge says he and Claude produced a version of the proof in Lean, a programming language that allows mathematical arguments to be checked by computer. Photo illustration: Reuters
A mathematician at AI company Anthropic said on Friday that he had used the firm’s Claude chatbot to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, a problem that has eluded mathematicians for more than 160 years.
“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Levent Alpoge wrote in a four-page note released on Friday.
The claim has not been independently verified, and the proof has not yet been reviewed by outside experts.
First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is widely regarded as the most important open question in pure mathematics.
It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, which offers US$1 million for a solution to each.
Under the institute’s rules, a solution must be published in a peer-reviewed journal and withstand two years of scrutiny.
Anthropic billboards are displayed in New York’s Times Square on Thursday, after the company’s IPO. Photo: AFP
Alpoge said the method also resolves a broader version of the problem known as the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis.
He said he and Claude had produced a version of the proof in Lean, a programming language that allows mathematical arguments to be checked by computer, and that he was releasing only that version for now.
A full written argument would be extremely long, he said, adding that he had not yet mastered all of the mathematics involved and planned to write it up properly.
Alpoge said he had consulted Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei before announcing the result, and acknowledged that its timing could be viewed cynically, without elaborating, although he was likely referring to this week’s record IPO.
In August, Anthropic said an unreleased version of Claude had improved a long-standing result related to the Riemann Hypothesis, while stressing that it had not proved it.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The claim comes two months after rival OpenAI said an AI model had solved another Millennium Prize Problem, on the equations that govern how fluids move. Mathematicians say that proof appears correct but has yet to be fully vetted.
Alpoge, who had worked on related fluid problems with New York University mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, was at the centre of a dispute over credit for that work. OpenAI denied wrongdoing.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Mamdani unveils plan to close New York’s notorious Rikers Island jail
content_en:
Plagued by violence and overcrowding, the complex has long stood as a symbol of dysfunction.
The Rikers Island jail complex stands in New York with the Manhattan skyline in the background in June 2014. Photo: AP
New York’s Rikers Island jail complex would close by 2032 under a sweeping plan announced on Friday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose strategy for finally shuttering the notorious facility hinges on substantially reducing the number of people kept behind bars.
The mayor, a Democrat, unveiled the plan as the city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027.
For years, Rikers Island has stood as a symbol of dysfunction, with the network of jails so plagued by violence and overcrowding that a federal judge, citing “abnormal and unacceptable” conditions, appointed an outside manager to restore order and implement reforms.
Mamdani has been a vocal proponent of closing Rikers, though the long-standing plan to build new jails has met fierce pushback, including from his predecessor, former mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and borough jails.
At a celebratory news conference at City Hall, Mamdani said the extended timeline was needed because of resistance from the previous administration, calling Rikers “a place we have long turned our eyes away from rather than confront head on”.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks to the media during a press briefing at Athens Square on Tuesday. Photo: dpa
“The call to close Rikers has echoed across our city for decades. Work has begun to do so, then stopped, then started once again. What will make this chapter different is our commitment to see it through,” he said.
The plan centres on a goal of lowering the city’s inmate population from the around 6,700 people currently housed at Rikers to a little over 4,000.
The Mamdani administration is proposing a new slate of diversion and supervised release programmes, expanding housing and social services to prevent recidivism, along with restoring an online bail payment system and reducing case delays so people spend less time behind bars.
“Our nation has a very real mass incarceration problem,” the mayor said. “We are making a conscious decision to advance a new model of a criminal legal system in our city, one that takes on that problem head on.”
Instead of housing prisoners at Rikers – an island in the East River near LaGuardia Airport – the city will shift people to jails in the Bronx, Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan, as well as a handful of medical facilities for people who need healthcare or psychiatric treatment.
The city also plans to reduce the number of beds for women, diverting them into community-based programmes.
A new jail is under construction in the Brooklyn borough of New York in October. Photo: AP
The borough jails are expected to open in Brooklyn in 2029; the Bronx and Queens in 2031; and then Manhattan in 2032, according to City Hall.
The new deadlines require approval from the New York City Council.
Julie Menin, speaker of the City Council, praised the mayor’s plan at the news conference, saying that after years of delay “we are finally getting back on track”.
The City Council voted to close the jail complex in 2019 and replace it with newer jails located in the city’s boroughs by 2027.
At the time, city officials had also called for shrinking the jail population to accommodate the closure, but ran into opposition from critics who argued doing so would mean more violent criminals on city streets.

title_display: Mamdani unveils plan to close New York’s notorious Rikers Island jail
content_display:
Plagued by violence and overcrowding, the complex has long stood as a symbol of dysfunction.
The Rikers Island jail complex stands in New York with the Manhattan skyline in the background in June 2014. Photo: AP
New York’s Rikers Island jail complex would close by 2032 under a sweeping plan announced on Friday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose strategy for finally shuttering the notorious facility hinges on substantially reducing the number of people kept behind bars.
The mayor, a Democrat, unveiled the plan as the city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027.
For years, Rikers Island has stood as a symbol of dysfunction, with the network of jails so plagued by violence and overcrowding that a federal judge, citing “abnormal and unacceptable” conditions, appointed an outside manager to restore order and implement reforms.
Mamdani has been a vocal proponent of closing Rikers, though the long-standing plan to build new jails has met fierce pushback, including from his predecessor, former mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and borough jails.
At a celebratory news conference at City Hall, Mamdani said the extended timeline was needed because of resistance from the previous administration, calling Rikers “a place we have long turned our eyes away from rather than confront head on”.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks to the media during a press briefing at Athens Square on Tuesday. Photo: dpa
“The call to close Rikers has echoed across our city for decades. Work has begun to do so, then stopped, then started once again. What will make this chapter different is our commitment to see it through,” he said.
The plan centres on a goal of lowering the city’s inmate population from the around 6,700 people currently housed at Rikers to a little over 4,000.
The Mamdani administration is proposing a new slate of diversion and supervised release programmes, expanding housing and social services to prevent recidivism, along with restoring an online bail payment system and reducing case delays so people spend less time behind bars.
“Our nation has a very real mass incarceration problem,” the mayor said. “We are making a conscious decision to advance a new model of a criminal legal system in our city, one that takes on that problem head on.”
Instead of housing prisoners at Rikers – an island in the East River near LaGuardia Airport – the city will shift people to jails in the Bronx, Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan, as well as a handful of medical facilities for people who need healthcare or psychiatric treatment.
The city also plans to reduce the number of beds for women, diverting them into community-based programmes.
A new jail is under construction in the Brooklyn borough of New York in October. Photo: AP
The borough jails are expected to open in Brooklyn in 2029; the Bronx and Queens in 2031; and then Manhattan in 2032, according to City Hall.
The new deadlines require approval from the New York City Council.
Julie Menin, speaker of the City Council, praised the mayor’s plan at the news conference, saying that after years of delay “we are finally getting back on track”.
The City Council voted to close the jail complex in 2019 and replace it with newer jails located in the city’s boroughs by 2027.
At the time, city officials had also called for shrinking the jail population to accommodate the closure, but ran into opposition from critics who argued doing so would mean more violent criminals on city streets.

title_en: Hong Kong slams ‘biased’ US report accusing city of expanding security powers
content_en:
Hong Kong government hits out at ‘slanders and smears’ in report by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission.
Hong Kong guarantees fundamental rights and freedoms, a government spokesman said. Photo: Karma Lo
Hong Kong has slammed an annual report by a US congressional commission that accused the government of expanding its security powers, including restricting media coverage of the Wang Fuk Court fire, the city’s deadliest blaze in decades.
The Hong Kong government on Friday evening condemned the report issued by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC) a day earlier, calling its accusations “biased slanders and smears”.
It urged the United States to “discern facts from fallacies” and stop interfering in Hong Kong affairs.
“The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government [on Friday] strongly condemns and must resolutely refute the untrue and biased slanders and smears against various aspects of the situation of the HKSAR,” it said.
The commission, a bipartisan panel established by the US Congress to assess the national security implications of US-China economic ties, accused the Hong Kong government of continuing to systematically expand executive and security powers over the past year.
It said Hong Kong had given “Beijing’s security offices a greater role in local processes, eliminating the legal predictability and judicial independence that previously distinguished the city from the rest of China”.
The report said: “Beijing’s successful imposition of the mainland security regime in Hong Kong remains basically unchecked. Hong Kong authorities have jailed or quelled through repression elements of civil society that had resisted.”
It also claimed that “Hong Kong continues to enable China’s support for autocratic regimes in Russia, Iran and North Korea by acting as a central nexus for sanctions and export control evasion”.
Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po was the scene of Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades. Photo: Dickson Lee
The report also pointed to the Wang Fuk Court blaze last year, saying that “press restrictions now appear to apply even when media coverage could help expose flagrant corruption that has led to major tragedies”.
The commission recommended that Congress require the US secretaries of state, treasury and commerce to jointly issue an annual Hong Kong business advisory telling US firms of the legal, regulatory, financial and reputational risks of operating in Hong Kong.
“Congress should enact legislation to apply Primary Money Laundering Concern special measures, including correspondent account prohibitions, on Hong Kong virtual asset service providers that fail to prevent Iranian, Russian or North Korean cryptocurrency trades,” it said in the report.
A government spokesman stressed that Hong Kong was an inalienable part of China and enjoyed a high degree of autonomy under “one country, two systems”, while coming directly under the central government.
“The legal basis for implementing ‘one country, two systems’ comprises the Constitution and the Basic Law, providing constitutional guarantees for fundamental rights and freedoms, including the right to equality before the law, and is buttressed by the rule of law and independent judicial power,” he said.
On the Wang Fuk Court blaze in Tai Po, the spokesman said the government had been pushing forward with the post-fire response with full force.
“Nonetheless, foreign forces and anti-China and destabilising forces with ulterior motives, after the fire, through disseminating fake news and false messages on the internet, and even distributing seditious pamphlets, et cetera, intended to maliciously smear the rescue work, instigate social division and conflict to undermine society’s unity in taking forward the support and relief work,” he added.
“The HKSAR government will not tolerate any act of malicious smearing and incitement of hatred, and will carry out decisive enforcement actions in accordance with the law.”
The spokesman said the government steadfastly safeguarded national sovereignty, security and development interests, and fully and faithfully upheld this top priority of the one country, two systems principle.
“The HKSAR government strongly urges the US to discern facts from fallacies, respect international law and basic norms governing international relations and immediately stop interfering in Hong Kong matters, which are purely China’s internal affairs,” he said.
By Fiona Sun

title_en: Russian missiles land in Poland, as Europe holds military drills nearby
content_en:
Nato called the act a violation, while Warsaw slammed the ‘intentional provocation’ by Moscow.
Surveillance camera footage posted on social media on Friday shows the flash of an explosion near Chmielek, in Bilgoraj County in eastern Poland. Photo: Social media via AFP
Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland on Friday in what its prime minister said was likely to be a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine.
The incidents occurred while Russia carried out a major nighttime bombardment of neighbouring Ukraine.
The development stoked tensions between Europe and Moscow just as the US is trying to add momentum to talks it is mediating on ending the war that began with Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared that “we are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Russia.
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the missiles and suspected drone, or on Friday’s drills.
A French soldier flies a drone at the Nowa Deba military training ground in Poland on Friday. Photo: AFP
One Russian missile is believed to have crashed around 35km (22 miles) from where the military exercises were taking place, officials said.
A Kh-101 cruise missile went down roughly 50km (30 miles) from the Ukraine border, and what officials believe was likely a jet-powered drone hit about 30km (20 miles) from the border with Ukraine.
There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage.
European troops were taking part on Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began November 9 in southeastern Poland. Forces are preparing for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilise the country and rebuild its military.
European countries have previously expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilise the continent.
US President Donald Trump discussed the war at a summit in China on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff.
Another envoy, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, told European leaders that the US believes Russia is “comfortable” with Nato-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine, in what could be a step towards compromise.
Polish soldiers take part in combat vehicle servicing and technical support during an exercise at the Nowa Deba military training ground on Friday. Photo: AFP
But Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said on Friday that even a quasi-membership in Nato for Ukraine would be unacceptable, Russia’s Interfax news agency reported.
“We discuss security guarantees primarily in terms of ensuring the security of our own country, and that’s what we’re talking about,” Ryabkov said.
Russia’s nighttime attack on Ukraine came hours after Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes this week on a bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. The bridge is vital to Moscow’s war effort.
Images from closed-circuit cameras and a mobile phone in the region collected by Poland’s PAP news agency showed a large, loud explosion and a bright flash, apparently in a wooded area, in one of the crashes.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte called the development in Poland a “grave violation” of that country’s airspace. “This incident is clearly dangerous – a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine,” Rutte said on social media.
Rutte is expected to go to Poland this weekend in response.
Under Nato’s collective security guarantee – Article 5 of its founding treaty – an attack on any ally should be considered an attack on all 32 members. It obliges members to provide support to that ally, most likely military backup, but does not limit them to that alone.
Article 5 is not triggered automatically. Ultimately, it is a political decision that all members must agree to. Poland also has the option to enact Article 4, which it did last year. This provides for emergency consultations only.
Flags fly as soldiers take part in a military exercise in Nowa Deba, Poland, on Friday. Photo: EPA
The development brought a chorus of European condemnation.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham described it as “utterly unacceptable”.
European Council President Antonio Costa said that Russia “continues to spread [its] threats”. Germany’s foreign ministry called it “yet another example of Russia’s ongoing provocations”.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the incident in Poland “demonstrates the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the transatlantic community”.
Later Friday, the chief of defence intelligence for the UK said he was confident that Russia “does not actively seek war with Nato”.
Lieutenant General Matthew Jones said in a speech at a college in Cambridge, his greatest fear was “the risk of a significant miscalculation”.
“There are too many recent examples of reckless Russian behaviour where, if the incident had been slightly different, the results could have been extremely serious,” said Jones, who did not directly mention the incidents in Poland.
Putin has said that Russia will not accept any European troops deployed to Ukraine after a prospective peace deal and will view them as legitimate targets.
By Associated Press

title_en: Princeton PhD student from China detained by ICE after US academic conference
content_en:
Eva Yi Xie, a third-year neuroscience student at the Ivy League university, was detained at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington.
Princeton University in New Jersey. Eva Yi Xie is a third-year neuroscience student at the prestigious Ivy League research institution. Photo: Shutterstock
A Chinese PhD student at Princeton University, New Jersey, was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Thursday after presenting her research at a neuroscience conference in Washington, the South China Morning Post has confirmed.
Eva Yi Xie, a third-year neuroscience student, was detained at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington while travelling home from the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting, according to a post on social media by her lab, the Brody Lab. It remains unclear why Xie was detained.
Since Xie’s detention, Princeton University has provided legal support.
“The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family and colleagues to provide support,” Rodney D. Priestley, dean of Princeton’s Graduate School, said in a statement to SCMP. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”
Priestley also said Xie’s detention distressed him and many members of the university community.
[embedded media]
The conference, which ended on November 18, is the field’s premier annual gathering, attracting more than 20,000 registrations from academia and industry. Several scholars said visa delays and other complications had prevented some attendees from taking part this year, raising concerns that restrictive immigration policies were hindering academic development.
An ICE detainee search returned one record for a Yi Xie, born in China, listed as being in custody. The record did not specify where she was being held. Brody Lab said she was being held in Chantilly, Virginia.
SCMP has contacted ICE for comment.
A spokesperson for Senator Andy Kim, a Democrat representing New Jersey, where Princeton is located, told SCMP that his office had been in direct contact with Xie and was “working diligently on her case”. The office declined to provide further details, citing privacy concerns.
Xie’s research involves the neural basis of decision-making, according to her personal website. A 2020 profile in her New York high school’s science publication said she had left Shanghai for the US in 2016 following what she described as an “overnight decision”.
She graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024 with degrees in computer science and mathematics and has interned at Meta, Microsoft AI and IBM Research.
The Brody Lab’s post, which urged supporters to help “bring her home”, had attracted more than 2.6 million views, 28,000 likes and 5,600 reposts, as of Friday afternoon.
The case also drew reactions from the technology industry. Jeff Dean, a former Google chief scientist who led the company’s AI research, said on social media that detaining a doctoral student returning from a conference where she had presented scientific research “is not how we get the best and brightest scientists in the world to want to come to the US”. He said he hoped the matter would be resolved quickly.
The Daily Princetonian, the university’s student newspaper, reported that Xie’s adviser, Carlos Brody, described her as a “law-abiding student” and questioned the rationale for her detention.
More scholars from overseas being detained in the US
Xie’s case comes amid a broader pattern of scholars being detained by immigration authorities while travelling to or from academic gatherings.
In July, Berhanu Kibret, an Ethiopian-born faculty member at the University of Maryland School of Pharmacy, was taken into custody at an airport after attending the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy’s annual conference in Dallas, where he received a teaching award.
Despite having legal employment authorisation, federal agents cited his expired visa status as the reason for his detention.
Similarly, University of Oklahoma Iranian studies scholar Vahid Abedini was stopped while travelling to Washington for the Middle East Studies Association’s annual convention.
Although he held a valid H-1B visa, officials detained him for several days before releasing him after widespread backlash from academics. Homeland Security officials later described the encounter as routine.
Concerns have also been raised about conditions inside ICE detention centres, many of which are operated by private prison companies under federal contracts.
By Ling Xin, Zhang Tong, Han Li

title_en: Can China’s top-down military adapt to the speed of AI and drone warfare?
content_en:
While commentaries in the military’s official newspaper draw lessons from Ukraine, analysts question how much Beijing will loosen its grip.
Illustration: Henry Wong
Drawing on lessons from the Ukraine war, Chinese military commentators are calling for frontline commanders to have greater freedom to make battlefield decisions without waiting for orders from above, as drones and AI accelerate the pace of combat.
Since July, several commentaries in the PLA Daily, the People’s Liberation Army’s official newspaper, have proposed ways to delegate tactical authority while keeping major military operations under centralised command.
This type of flexibility resembles the Western military concept of “mission command”, under which senior officers set objectives while allowing subordinate commanders to decide how to carry them out, particularly when battlefield conditions change or communications are disrupted.
[embedded media]
Analysts said the articles reflected long-standing Chinese military interest in more flexible battlefield decision-making and lessons from recent conflicts, but questioned how far such proposals could be implemented within China’s tightly controlled military system.
In one of the earliest commentaries, published in the PLA Daily on July 30, the authors described mission command as the “basic mode of distributed operations”, in which military units operate separately across a battlefield.
They argued that such troops needed to “make decisions independently” when they could not receive real-time instructions from higher headquarters. Those decisions, however, should continue to follow the “strategic intent of higher command”.
A more detailed proposal appeared in a PLA Daily article on October 18. It called for the authority of frontline units to be automatically adjusted as battlefield conditions changed.
Drawing on unnamed recent conflicts, the authors said rigid command arrangements had caused forces to “miss opportunities”, citing delays when troops had to seek approval “level by level” before striking targets.
But delays were not the only concern. The commentators also said that large, fixed command centres were becoming increasingly vulnerable to surveillance and long-range precision strikes. Destroying command centres early in a conflict could disrupt communications, delay orders and leave subordinate units struggling to coordinate operations.
Time has become a scarcer tactical resource than firepowerPLA Daily commentary
Militaries engaged in recent conflicts had consequently moved towards smaller, more dispersed and mobile headquarters, they noted. Such arrangements, combined with greater delegation of authority, could help forces continue operating, even if their command infrastructure came under attack, rather than simply allowing them to make decisions faster.

title_en: US embassy steps up attack on China over cartel meth as Mexico signs deals with Beijing
content_en:
Mexico’s Sheinbaum met Xi at the Apec summit in Shenzhen but ruled out a free-trade pact, leaving tariffs of up to 50 per cent in place.
Barrels of precursor chemicals shipped from China and allegedly destined for Mexico’s Sinaloa Cartel after their seizure by US authorities in September 2025. Photo: US Department of Justice
The US embassy in Mexico accused China on Thursday of supplying Mexican cartels with chemicals used to make methamphetamine, on the same day President Claudia Sheinbaum wrapped up a visit to Shenzhen during which she signed cooperation agreements with Beijing covering energy, science and the environment.
The embassy cited the US Department of Justice in a social media post and referred to chemicals bound for the Sinaloa Cartel that US Homeland Security Investigations seized in September last year.
“Different drug, same origin of the precursors: China. In just ONE WEEK in September 2025, US authorities (HSI) seized more than 300 tonnes of precursor chemicals from China destined for the Sinaloa cartel in Mexico,” the embassy said.
“These chemicals could have been used to make almost 190,000 kilos of methamphetamine, with an estimated value of US$569 million. It is not just about fentanyl. China is also a major source of precursor chemicals used to produce other synthetic drugs, such as methamphetamine.”
🚨 Distinta droga, mismo origen de los precursores: China. 🇨🇳
En tan solo UNA SEMANA de septiembre de 2025, autoridades estadounidenses (HSI) decomisaron más de 300 toneladas de precursores químicos procedentes de China, destinados al Cártel de Sinaloa en México. 🇲🇽
💊Estos… pic.twitter.com/TP2eUjWaAp
— Embajada de EE.UU. en México (@USEmbassyMEX) November 19, 2026
It was the second time during Sheinbaum’s visit that the US mission had singled out China over synthetic drugs.
On Tuesday, the day she met President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, the embassy posted that “fentanyl does not start in Mexico” and that its ingredients come mainly from China.
The Chinese embassy in Mexico responded within hours and accused its US counterpart of “defaming China”.
“It is worth asking whether this diplomatic mission is really fulfilling its functions on behalf of the US government, and whether it can handle matters with an objective attitude that respects the truth,” it said, adding that the fentanyl problem in the US “lies in its own regulatory deficiencies and drug abuse”.
The Chinese embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday’s post.
The two missions clashed in a similar way in September, when the US embassy marked Mexico’s independence day with the slogan “Viva Mexico, Made in China”. The Chinese embassy replied at the time that “someone is sowing discord”.
Meeting in Shenzhen
Sheinbaum travelled to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ summit and had said beforehand that trade would not be the main subject of her talks with Xi.
The Chinese president told Sheinbaum that taking relations “to new heights, across broader areas and in greater depth” was of great significance to promoting cooperation among Global South countries.
Sheinbaum told reporters they had discussed increasing Mexican exports to China “from avocados to tequila”.
Under an energy agreement, the two governments will develop solar thermal and geothermal power projects, with Chinese specialists training Mexican technicians. They also ratified 36 tourism twinning agreements and are working on a medical training memorandum.
“It is a new era ... of cooperation that allows us to improve the relationship and learn from the advances China has made, and also for China to learn about what we are doing in Mexico,” Sheinbaum told reporters before leaving Shenzhen.
She ruled out a free-trade agreement with China and said Mexico’s economic integration with the United States “is very large”.
“We already have a very large trade relationship [with China], so it is not our interest to move towards a free-trade agreement, but we do want to advance cooperation in different areas,” she said.
Tariffs and trade review
Trade has strained the relationship more than any other issue this year because Mexico began charging tariffs of 5 to 50 per cent in January on 1,463 categories of goods from countries without a trade agreement with it, including China.
Beijing concluded an investigation in March that found the duties were trade barriers affecting more than US$30 billion of its exports and threatened retaliation.
Mexico also shelved a BYD plant under US pressure. In July, Washington declined to extend the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which has governed trade across North America since 2020. The pact now faces annual reviews until it expires in 2036 unless the three governments reach a deal.
Limiting Chinese access to the North American market has become the main US demand in the talks.
Sheinbaum met US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the summit to discuss non-tariff barriers and trade negotiations, telling reporters that Mexico’s cooperation with China “will not affect” its relationship with Washington.
By Igor Patrick

title_en: America’s electoral blue wave brings only the illusion of change
content_en:
Despite the resurgence of the Democrats, the world should keep hedging against the US.
Incoming Congress members (from left) Jeremy Moss, Melat Kiros, Denise Powell and Don Leonard take a selfie as they arrive along with other congressional freshmen for a group photograph on the steps of the House of Representatives of the Capitol Building on November 12 in Washington. Photo: Getty Images via AFP
Don’t expect the Democratic blue wave to reverse the catastrophic decline in America’s global standing and domestic governance. That decline is structural and often self-inflicted.
As Paul Krugman said in a recent podcast, “Two years of Trump have led to a catastrophic decline in America’s global role. Around the world, America is neither loved nor feared. The world has learned that we can’t be trusted to honour our promises or defend our allies.”
“At the same time,” he continued, “we seem unable to punish our enemies. We have essentially lost a military war with Iran, a trade war with China. We may well be losing a technology race with China, too.”
Perhaps he exaggerates; America can still take on weak enemies like Cuba and Venezuela.
Meanwhile, the old Democratic establishment is already reasserting control over the party to ensure the progressives and democratic socialists who delivered the winning votes are sidelined when the new Congress opens. The young Turks were allowed to promise change. Once the old guard restores the status quo, though, voters will end up with more of the same.
A week after the midterms, the House voted on whether to advance the impeachment of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, in effect a verdict on the Iran war. Republicans prevailed 211 to 204 on a motion to send the impeachment resolution to the judiciary committee, effectively shelving it. Eleven Democrats did not show up. Had they voted, the outcome would have been different and impeachment could have proceeded. Democratic voters overwhelmingly oppose the Iran war.
Former House speaker Nancy Pelosi speaks to the media in the Longworth House Office Building on November 10 in Washington. Pelosi was among the 11 Democrats who missed the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote that night; she had left Washington to receive an award in San Francisco. Photo: Getty Images via AFP
The establishment intends to keep Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer as leaders of the House and Senate. Polls show both are hugely unpopular. Many Democratic newcomers ran on getting foreign and corporate money out of politics and rethinking military support for foreign nations.
Incoming congressman Don Leonard wanted to know where Jeffries stood before backing him as speaker. Leonard’s priorities were a constitutional amendment to end Citizens United – a ruling that allowed unlimited political donations – and an end to US support for the Iran war and Israel, which many Americans blame for the war. Instead, he got a lesson in how Washington works. Senior House Democrats, he said, told him that withholding support would mean “making my life a living hell for the next two years” and losing his seat.
Democrats were elected to hold politicians accountable, root out corruption and improve people’s daily lives. That this is shaping up to be an uphill battle rather than the bare minimum exposes the dismal state of US democracy.
Trump has shown an American president can resemble a Roman dictator more than a modern democratic leader. Both offices gave a republic temporary but almost absolute leadership without reinstating an absolute monarchy. Both concentrate executive decision-making in one person: Rome temporarily placed a single commander above its two consuls; America’s founders created a single president. Both hold supreme command of the armed forces in wartime.
If someone were genuinely threatening to tear apart the networks of influence, expose corruption, pursue accountability … there would be attack ads before breakfast, manufactured scandals by lunchtime and 17 billionaires crying about the end of civilisation before dinnerCarina Cedrechi
In theory, their powers are limited. Neither office was meant to be held for life: a dictator served six months; a president serves at most two four-year terms, at least since Franklin D. Roosevelt. Neither controls the treasury. But Trump has shown that a president with a subservient Congress can do as he pleases, just as Augustus, Rome’s first emperor, played the Senate like a fiddle while pretending to respect it.
The “Overton window” refers to the range of acceptable political debate, which drifts left or right over time. Voters want the Democrats – for lack of a better choice – to work outside that window. The Democratic elders will make sure that won’t happen.
As political YouTuber Carina Cedrechi puts it: “If someone were genuinely threatening to tear apart the networks of influence, expose corruption, pursue accountability regardless of party, and drag powerful people before the law, I suspect we’d be witnessing a political DEFCON 1.
“There would be attack ads before breakfast, manufactured scandals by lunchtime and 17 billionaires crying about the end of civilisation before dinner. The media would be having a collective nervous breakdown. Every microphone in Washington would be overheating. But Hakeem and Chuck, where’s the panic? Where’s the extraordinary resistance from these supposedly terrified power brokers?”
US President Donald Trump hosts a luncheon for tech leaders in the East Room of the White House in Washington on September 29. Photo: Reuters
Corruption is not confined to the Trump family or Republicans; it includes Democrats too. Recent actions and statements from the Democratic leadership are alarming.
America’s allies should likewise temper expectations of this Democratic majority. In the US’ two-party system, Republicans will return to power sooner or later.
Those who hope for this blue wave to restore responsible government and America’s global pre-eminence are likely to be disappointed. Other countries should stay the course: building relationships with one another and hedging with China.
By Alex Lo

The young Turks were allowed to promise change. Once the old guard restores the status quo, though, voters will end up with more of the same.

Had they voted, the outcome would have been different and impeachment could have proceeded. Democratic voters overwhelmingly oppose the Iran war.
Former House speaker Nancy Pelosi speaks to the media in the Longworth House Office Building on November 10 in Washington. Democrats were elected to hold politicians accountable, root out corruption and improve people’s daily lives. That this is shaping up to be an uphill battle rather than the bare minimum exposes the dismal state of US democracy.
Trump has shown an American president can resemble a Roman dictator more than a modern democratic leader. Both offices gave a republic temporary but almost absolute leadership without reinstating an absolute monarchy. Both concentrate executive decision-making in one person: Rome temporarily placed a single commander above its two consuls; America’s founders created a single president. Both hold supreme command of the armed forces in wartime.

The “Overton window” refers to the range of acceptable political debate, which drifts left or right over time. Voters want the Democrats – for lack of a better choice – to work outside that window. The Democratic elders will make sure that won’t happen.

Corruption is not confined to the Trump family or Republicans; it includes Democrats too. Recent actions and statements from the Democratic leadership are alarming.
America’s allies should likewise temper expectations of this Democratic majority. In the US’ two-party system, Republicans will return to power sooner or later.
Those who hope for this blue wave to restore responsible government and America’s global pre-eminence are likely to be disappointed. Other countries should stay the course: building relationships with one another and hedging with China.

title_en: Trump replaces US cyber chief after outages hit flights, banks and NSA
content_en:
Pentagon’s Kirsten Davies takes over in an acting role as US president says ousted Sean Cairncross was not ‘good enough’.
Kirsten Davies has replaced National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross after a wave of technology outages hit major US companies and government agencies. Photo: AP
US President Donald Trump has tapped the Pentagon’s chief information officer as his new cyber chief following a series of major outages that disrupted air travel, banking and classified communications, saying on Friday that her predecessor was not “good enough”.
Kirsten Davies will serve as acting national cyber director, replacing Sean Cairncross, who was dismissed on Thursday. She would need Senate confirmation to hold the post permanently.
Asked at a White House press conference on Friday why he had fired Cairncross, Trump replied: “Because I didn’t think that person was good enough.”
Trump said the air traffic control disruption and the bank systems failure were “all separate events” and “all under control”.
He attributed the banking problems to routine upgrades, while blaming ageing infrastructure for the aviation disruption. He urged the US Congress to approve US$50 billion to modernise the air traffic control system.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio had earlier said there was no evidence that the outages were connected or caused by hackers or other malicious actors.
US President Donald Trump speaks at the White House in Washington on Friday. During the news conference he said Cairncross was being replaced because he was not “good enough”. Photo: dpa
On November 12, a global Microsoft 365 outage disrupted services for businesses and government agencies.
The following day, the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures nationwide after telecommunications problems destabilised air traffic control communications and radar feeds. The ground stop lasted nearly five hours.
On November 16, JPMorgan Chase experienced a systems failure that delayed transactions for many customers. A day later, NSANet, the National Security Agency’s internal classified communications network, was disrupted. Apple’s iCloud login and other online services were disrupted the same day.
The Office of the National Cyber Director coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Cairncross, a former chief legal counsel at the Republican National Committee, had led the office since August last year.
Davies became the Pentagon’s chief information officer in December last year, overseeing its information technology and cybersecurity strategy, including efforts to modernise military networks.
In written answers to the Senate Armed Services Committee before her confirmation hearing in September last year, Davies pledged to strengthen military communications to outpace “near-peer adversaries like China and Russia, who are rapidly advancing their cyber and space-based capabilities”.
She also said China had invested heavily over decades in electromagnetic spectrum capabilities “designed to undermine US military superiority”.
Before entering government, she served as chief information security officer at Unilever and The Estee Lauder Companies, and held senior security roles at Barclays Africa Group, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens.
Writing on social media on Friday, Davies said: “Under President Trump’s leadership, we will have a more secure, resilient and supercharged technological future.”

title_en: Hong Kong’s dim sum bond index will sustain global yuan momentum
content_en:
The new benchmark fills a gap in the city’s offshore renminbi ecosystem – just what a maturing financial market needs.
Beijing is intensifying its efforts to internationalise the yuan and reduce reliance on a US dollar-dominated financial architecture amid geopolitical tensions. Photo: Reuters
Hong Kong’s first bond index for offshore yuan debt marks an important step in the city’s effort to further strengthen its status as the premier offshore renminbi centre. The HKEX Offshore RMB Bond Index, launched by Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, tracks the performance of offshore yuan-denominated bonds, also known as dim sum bonds.
As Kevin Fan, head of FIC product development at HKEX, noted, the index is “an important element of establishing a complete ecosystem for the bond market in Hong Kong”. It lets investors track performance and allows financial firms to build exchange-traded funds and other derivatives, encouraging the issuance and trading of dim sum bonds.
The index includes dim sum bonds listed on the HKEX stock exchange or held by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Central Moneymarkets Unit. Bonds need a minimum issue size of 1 billion yuan and a maturity of more than one year; those falling below the one-year threshold will be removed. As of October 30, it covered 305 bonds with a combined market valuation of 864 billion yuan (US$130 billion), an average yield of 2.08 per cent and an average tenure of 4.7 years. Sub-indexes based on duration and credit rating will allow fund providers to create different types of ETFs as it operates in a transparent way to measure the performance of the dim sum bond market.
The task now is to ensure that ETF providers, issuers and investors make full use of it.
The timing reflects a rapidly expanding market supported by the necessary technical infrastructure. Dim sum bond issuance reached 590 billion yuan in the first nine months of this year, surpassing the 448 billion yuan issued in all of last year and the previous annual record of 475 billion yuan set in 2024. The 2017 total, by comparison, was just 29 billion yuan.
HKEX now serves as the listing venue for 68 per cent of dim sum bonds issued this year, up from 47 per cent in 2017. Notably, Hong Kong’s listed bond issuance in offshore yuan has surpassed US dollar-denominated sales for the first time. Dim sum issuance on HKEX climbed to 342 billion yuan in the first 10 months, or 42 per cent of total listed bond issuance, against 30 per cent for US dollar bonds, 16 per cent for Hong Kong dollar bonds and 12 per cent for other currencies.
At the launch, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said the city’s offshore renminbi ecosystem “is now largely in place”, with tools to invest, measure performance and manage risk available in one market. Also available are yuan counters for Hong Kong stocks, with authorities working to include them in southbound Stock Connect; the Bond Connect; the Swap Connect; and China government bond futures, whose trade volume has exceeded 50 billion yuan within three months of launch. Together, they form a coherent architecture. The index is, in Chan’s words, “an important piece in the puzzle”.
Beijing is intensifying efforts to internationalise the yuan and reduce reliance on a US dollar-dominated financial architecture amid geopolitical tensions, priorities reiterated in the People’s Bank of China’s recent five-year blueprint and Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s September policy address. Hong Kong handled 76 per cent of global offshore yuan payments as of October, according to Swift, and its banking system held more than 1.13 trillion yuan in deposits as of September, the largest offshore yuan liquidity pool outside the mainland.
The city is, at long last, achieving its ambition with the growing depth and sophistication of yuan-related activity. Chan adds a further dimension: with rates elevated in many advanced economies, the yuan is becoming an attractive alternative as a cost-competitive funding currency for global issuers as well as an asset for international investors.
A benchmark is the foundation on which a deeper market is built. The index arrives with strong interest from ETF issuers, and a dozen asset managers are already preparing linked products. As those funds come to market, secondary trading in dim sum bonds should broaden, giving global investors convenient, diversified access to yuan assets. Sustaining the momentum behind the 109 HKEX-listed issuances recorded in the first 10 months will reinforce that virtuous cycle. Measurable, transparent and investible, the index supplies what a maturing market requires.
By SCMP Editorial

title_en: A steadier US-China relationship still leaves Southeast Asia on guard
content_en:
The terms of any bilateral compact matter more than stability itself – and whether the region has any say over them.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in the Rose Garden of the White House on September 24. Photo: AFP
Even as Washington and Beijing seek greater stability in their relationship, tensions involving China and US allies and partners in Southeast Asia can and do persist. On September 24, while Chinese President Xi Jinping was on a state visit to Washington, another incident unfolded around Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea, with Manila and Beijing offering different accounts. This captures a broader regional reality: US-China stabilisation may lower some risks but raise others and leave long-standing disputes unrelieved.
The effort to stabilise ties with China is part of a broader US turn towards selective accommodation with major adversaries, mainly through leader-level bargaining. On October 16, US President Donald Trump waived most of the new Russia sanctions under a law he had signed a month earlier. In August, he scaled back joint exercises with South Korea, citing his relationship with Kim Jong-un – and has repeatedly said he is open to meeting Kim again. None of this amounts to a comprehensive settlement or a consistent policy towards Beijing, Moscow and Pyongyang. Rather, it suggests Trump’s willingness to ease pressure on these countries in pursuit of direct engagement with their leaders, and to adjust security arrangements with US allies in the process.
For Southeast Asia, such accommodation may reduce the risk of great power confrontation, but it also increases uncertainty about whether the region’s interests will be adequately factored into bargains struck between Washington and Beijing.
Two variables will shape the outcome: how durable US-China stabilisation proves and how robust Washington’s commitment to the region remains. For now, the likeliest combination is a steadier US-China relationship alongside an America that stays engaged but is increasingly stretched and less predictable.
The BRP Sierra Madre, a World War II-era warship deliberately grounded by the Philippines at Second Thomas Shoal in 1999 to reinforce its territorial claim in the South China Sea. Photo: AFP
Steady stabilisation?
There are grounds to expect stability to hold. During Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, Xi set out a new vision of “constructive strategic stability” intended to guide US-China relations. Xi’s September visit to Washington extended the trade truce to January 10, 2027, recommended favourable tariff treatment for US$30 billion of goods in each direction and confirmed plans for two more leader-level meetings before the end of the year.
This has three implications for Southeast Asia.
First, sustained dialogue between Washington and Beijing can reduce the danger of military confrontation and disruptive economic escalation, both long-standing regional concerns.
Second, bilateral bargaining carries a risk of excluding the region. Washington and Beijing may reach understandings that affect Southeast Asian interests while leaving regional governments with little influence over the outcome. So far, the most consequential forms of this have not materialised. Washington has not formally changed its Taiwan policy, nor struck the sweeping US-China trade deal that Southeast Asian exporters feared would leave them at a disadvantage. But the reciprocal tariff cuts recommended after Xi’s September visit would, once implemented, narrow Southeast Asia’s tariff advantage over China in the sectors covered.
Third, stabilisation does not resolve China’s disputes with Southeast Asian states. As the September 24 incident illustrates, a more stable US-China relationship can coexist with continuing tensions in the South China Sea.
American commitment
The second variable is the scope and reliability of US commitment to the region. Here, America’s declared priorities and available resources do not always align. In August, Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s undersecretary for policy, said the department remained focused on the first island chain, including the Philippines. Yet, at the time, the redeployment of the USS George Washington to the Middle East left no US carrier strike group west of San Diego.
The US Navy aircraft carrier USS George Washington patrols waters west of the Korean peninsula. Its redeployment to the Middle East left the western Pacific temporarily without a US carrier strike group. Photo: US Navy
The carrier was expected back by early November, yet remained in the Arabian Sea past the middle of the month until its return to the US Navy’s Seventh Fleet area of operations in the Asia-Pacific was finally confirmed on Wednesday. Washington may name the first island chain as a priority in its National Security Strategy and National Defence Strategy, yet still diverts finite military resources to competing theatres.
Southeast Asian nations will view these developments through different lenses, depending on their vulnerabilities. The latest ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute State of Southeast Asia survey, conducted in January-February 2026, captures these underlying concerns. The South China Sea topped Philippine respondents’ geopolitical concerns, with 55 per cent expecting their country’s relations with China to worsen. Singaporean, Thai and Cambodian respondents, meanwhile, ranked economic tensions between major powers as their top regional challenge. US-China stabilisation resolves neither concern.
For Manila, tensions with China have not receded. For economically exposed states, avoiding a US-China trade war is welcome, but less so if tariff relief for China narrows their own tariff advantage and attractiveness as alternative investment destinations. What matters is less stabilisation itself than the terms on which it occurs – and how Washington and Beijing behave under it.
Policy implications
Southeast Asian states are not simply passive recipients of these outcomes. They have widened their room for manoeuvre by diversifying relationships, a preference the region broadly shares: 55.2 per cent of ISEAS survey respondents favoured strengthening Asean resilience and unity in navigating great power rivalry, while only 6.3 per cent thought the region must choose a side. Indonesia, for example, has concluded trade negotiations with the European Union and signed a trade agreement with the US, while conducting military exercises with China, Russia and the US.
Southeast Asian leaders and representatives link hands during the opening of the 49th Asean Summit in Manila, Philippines, on Sunday. Photo: Reuters
Room for manoeuvre means securing useful commitments from several partners without exclusive alignment. But it matters only if it translates into influence over decisions that affect the region, which requires states to retain their rights and a meaningful role in arrangements affecting their interests. They can press their case bilaterally with major powers and collectively through the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, whose 11 members’ combined voice should carry greater weight. Yet the bilateral ties that broaden a nation’s options can also make Asean cohesion harder to sustain.
The South China Sea code of conduct talks, which have reached provisional agreement on between 85 and 90 per cent of the draft, according to Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, will still carry over into 2027 and raise precisely this question: can Asean negotiate meaningful rules with China when its members’ relations with Beijing, Washington and other external powers are increasingly divergent?
US-China stabilisation is preferable to confrontation, but it does not by itself automatically produce security for Southeast Asia. Much will depend on the terms of their accommodation, how both major powers behave towards the region and whether Southeast Asian states can retain meaningful influence over the decisions that affect them.

title_en: AI agents are getting wallets. Is Hong Kong ready for them?
content_en:
As city pushes for agentic commerce, autonomous systems that can browse, compare and complete purchases on their own are starting to emerge.
The core premise of Minds, created by Web3 firm Animoca Brands, is to build an AI companion that can handle tasks ranging from hotel bookings to reservations to online retail. Photo: Handout
Minds by Animoca Brands, an agentic artificial intelligence platform created by the Web3 firm, is riding on Hong Kong’s push to turn automated agents into everyday shopping tools, piloting live transactions on Visa’s network just as local regulators place agentic commerce on the policy agenda.
Unlike conventional chatbots that merely answer user questions about products, agentic commerce relies on autonomous AI systems capable of browsing, comparing options and executing payments on a user’s behalf within pre-set guard rails.
“Everyone who works on agentic stuff today knows for certain that the agentic commerce pie will grow – we don’t have any doubts about this,” said Minh Do, chief operating officer of Animoca Brands, in a recent interview with the South China Morning Post.
Industry forecasts reflect that optimism. In April, Juniper Research projected global agentic commerce transaction value would surge from about US$8 billion this year to US$1.5 trillion by 2030.
Over the same period, McKinsey estimated US$3 trillion to US$5 trillion in global consumer retail revenue could be orchestrated through agents, while Bain expected fully agentic sales in the United States to reach US$300 billion to US$500 billion, or 15 to 25 per cent of American e-commerce.
For Hong Kong, however, Do struck a more conservative tone, saying mainstream adoption would take time: about two years for consumers in their 40s and around five for those over 60.
“Agentic commerce is very early, and it will grow through small, specific pockets first, not through mass consumer purchases like groceries,” Do said, declining to estimate the local market size.
He expected early momentum to come from niche, high-engagement communities, such as Pokemon card collectors trading on Collector Crypt, a digital marketplace and vault on the Solana blockchain that tokenises physical cards into redeemable non-fungible tokens.
That would be followed by buyers of digital commodities including data sets, domains and software access, Do said.
To attract such users, Minds pairs practical shopping tools with a game-like interface. Its core premise is to build an AI companion that can handle tasks ranging from hotel bookings to reservations to online retail.
[embedded media]
Animoca Brands has spent recent months integrating that consumer experience into established payment systems.
In July, it launched a live pilot with Visa in which Minds finds card offers and completes purchases using Visa Intelligent Commerce tokens, debuting on the online shop of the Bruce Lee Club, a Hong Kong fan club and memorabilia group dedicated to the late martial arts icon.
Users set spending limits, while the agent had no access to credit card numbers, according to the companies.
In October, Minds teamed up with Animoca Brands’ digital identity unit Moca Network, fintech firm Reap and AI shopping infrastructure start-up Pivota to design a credential system that capped spending by store, amount and time.
Those safeguards mirror the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s regulatory blueprint.
Earlier this month at Hong Kong Fintech Week, the de facto central bank unveiled Sage – or Securing Agentic Finance with Governance and Enablement – forming a cross-sector advisory group that includes Animoca Brands alongside a discussion paper on how banks should govern autonomous AI transactions.
Even with regulatory backing, however, Animoca Brands is entering a market where payment incumbents have already laid some of the groundwork.
Mastercard completed Hong Kong’s first live, authenticated agentic transaction in March – an airport transfer booked through service provider Hoppa by an agent built by CardInfoLink, with HSBC and DBS Bank (Hong Kong) as partners.
DBS also described itself as the first bank in the Asia-Pacific region to pilot Visa Intelligent Commerce, while Visa’s agent-readiness programme was already operating in the city.
Minds’ edge, however, could lie on the consumer side: offering a local interface for shoppers rather than the underlying payments infrastructure.
In comparison, mainland China’s tech giants appear to be scaling up more rapidly.
Ant Group’s Alipay said its AI Pay had processed 300 million agent payments by late May, and in August launched a merchant platform designed to convert standard online storefronts into machine-readable plug-ins that AI agents can browse and buy from directly.
Ant Group is a fintech affiliate of Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post.
Tencent Holdings’ Yuanbao links to e-commerce platform JD.com’s mini-program ecosystem, though users still complete checkout manually, while Tenpay recently signed memorandums of understanding with Visa and Mastercard to bring agentic commerce to international wallets.
Daniel Hong, vice-president of Tencent Financial Technology, said the roll-out would eventually allow foreign visitors to manage trip planning, hotel bookings and ride-hailing in a single flow.
By Christina Zhao

title_en: Nvidia faces further blow after shock US export permit data release: analysts
content_en:
Revelation that Washington approved export of nearly 880,000 advanced chips to China could put further pressure on Nvidia, analysts say.
Chinese tech companies are likely to pivot from Nvidia to Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) amid intense scrutiny of chip exports in Washington, analysts say. Photo: Shutterstock
US lawmakers have thrown the cross-border semiconductor trade into fresh turmoil after releasing confidential licensing records showing Washington approved the sale of nearly 880,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese tech companies earlier this year.
The disclosures, made by a US House committee on Thursday, could prompt Chinese buyers to pivot from Nvidia to Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) in the short term and accelerate their transition to home-made chips over the long run, analysts said.
The filing showed that US officials had granted permission for nearly 880,000 artificial intelligence processors – specifically Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s MI325X chips – to be sold to Chinese firms out of 3.4 million total requests as of May 11.
The publication of the sensitive export data, combined with Nvidia’s abrupt retreat amid intense political scrutiny of its China ties, is expected to have an immediate impact on Chinese technology companies, according to analysts.
Shi Shenchang, a compliance lawyer at Shanghai-based Co-Effort Law Firm, said the Chinese companies named in the disclosures would likely pivot towards AMD, whose flagship MI325X served as a major alternative to Nvidia’s H200 for training and running large AI models.
However, he warned that AMD would struggle to fill the supply gap in the short run, noting that scaling up procurement hinged on stable deliveries and software adaptation.
Even that workaround may prove short-lived, according to Chen Yun, a Beijing-based independent semiconductor analyst.
“It is expected that AMD’s licences will eventually be revoked in the future, just as Nvidia stated they are stopping H200 sales to China,” Chen said.
With top-tier US hardware such as Nvidia’s Blackwell B300 series completely barred from sale to China, tighter enforcement could leave grey-market channels as the only way to obtain cutting-edge Western chips, Chen added.
“If they don’t smuggle, they can only rely on domestic chips. But smuggling is extremely expensive,” he said, noting that black-market prices for a single B300 unit had surged past 20 million yuan (US$2.8 million) in China.
Washington granted permission for Nvidia’s H200 processor to be exported to China on a case-by-case basis in January, but Nvidia has now suspended sales to Chinese buyers. Photo: Handout
The revelations land at a moment of upheaval for Nvidia, which is scrambling to steady its operations following the resignation of co-founder and former chief executive Jensen Huang and Washington’s tightening of controls over Chinese companies’ access to AI compute via third countries.
Earlier this week, Nvidia interim CEO and finance chief Colette Kress said the company had halted shipments of licensed Hopper data-centre products to China – a business line that generated US$2.4 billion in the recent October quarter alone.
That freeze includes sales of the H200 processors initially permitted under a case-by-case Commerce Department review policy introduced in January.
Still, legal and industry observers cautioned that the headline approval figures could overstate how much US computing power had actually come online in China. While regulators initially cleared nearly 580,000 H200 units for export, getting the hardware operational might take months, Shi noted.
“US export licences only solve the problem of whether they can be exported,” he said, pointing out that pre-shipment inspections, customs clearance and system debugging meant most of the approved chips were likely not yet deployed at scale.
The approved recipients include firms on the US Department of Defence’s Chinese Military Companies list, such as Alibaba Group Holding, Tencent Holdings and Baidu.
Alibaba and its subsidiaries sought to acquire 948,950 chips, with the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) approving 75,000 of those sales under an application Nvidia filed in December. BIS returned the remaining requests, including one for 610,000 units, without action. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
Tencent and its subsidiaries aimed to purchase 150,000 chips, ByteDance and its subsidiary 150,000, Baidu 43,000 and JD.com 41,300. None of the five companies immediately responded to requests for comment on Friday.
Ultimately, prolonged US vetting and delivery bottlenecks were pushing Chinese buyers inward, according to Shanghai-based foreign-affairs lawyers Chen Hui and Jiang Wanting.
“Changes in US licensing policies may affect short-term transaction opportunities, but they can hardly determine the long-term landscape of China’s AI chip market alone,” they said, adding that domestic AI accelerator makers were offering increasingly viable alternatives as the local ecosystem matured.
By Ann Cao
