title_en: Tanks, drone and anti-drone vehicles spotted at Zhuhai air show site
content_en:
Hardware seen in images and videos posted online reflects push to integrate hi-tech platforms on battlefields and defence market ambitions.
A smaller unmanned combat vehicle equipped with Hongjian missiles was seen at the Zhuhai air show site, according to unverified videos posted on social media. Photo: X/ WenJian0922
New vehicles for drone and anti-drone warfare have been spotted at the site where the Zhuhai air show will be held next month, reflecting China’s push to integrate hi-tech platforms on land battlefields as well as its ambitions in the global defence market.
Images and videos circulating online show hardware including two unmanned combat vehicles – one equipped with Hongjian missiles – and a new type of anti-drone tactical vehicle at the site in southeastern China where the air show will be held from December 7 to 13.
The images and videos have not been independently verified by the South China Morning Post.
The anti-drone tactical vehicle is a six-wheeled Dongfeng Mengshi-III off-road armoured vehicle with a large active electronically scanned array – or AESA – radar.
Social media images from Tuesday showed the big mushroom-shaped AESA radar at the back of the vehicle, with an arm to adjust its position.
An image posted to social media appears to show the Mengshi-III anti-drone tactical armoured vehicle with mushroom-shaped AESA rader. Photo: qq.com
Military bloggers suggested the AESA radar could have an anti-drone function and that it had a detection range of 10km (6.2 miles) for low-altitude objects. They also said the Mengshi-III variant in the images revealed part of China’s counter-unmanned aircraft systems (C-UAS). It is not known whether the vehicle is for export or not.
The AESA is among the most advanced radar technology China uses and exports. The radars use electronically steered beams to scan for targets, allowing them to detect and track multiple objects simultaneously without relying on mechanical antenna rotation.
These capabilities are particularly valuable in counter-drone operations, where systems must rapidly identify and track small, low-flying and agile targets.
Drones have become widely used in modern warfare – from the Russia-Ukraine war to the Iran war – and like others, China’s military has been working on counter-drone equipment and training across its forces.
China has also emerged as one of the world’s leading exporters of military drones in the last decade – supplying them across the Middle East, Africa and Asia – and the Zhuhai air show provides a platform to show its hardware to the international defence market.
[embedded media]
A smaller unmanned combat vehicle equipped with Hongjian missiles was also at the air show site, according to videos posted on social media on Monday by Chinese military bloggers.
The vehicle had four missiles from the Hongjian series but the type was not known.
State broadcaster CCTV reported on a similar unmanned vehicle in August which it said carried Hongjian-73 anti-tank guided missiles.
The armed unmanned ground vehicles reflect an effort to introduce robotic platforms into land warfare, potentially allowing troops to conduct reconnaissance, transport supplies and engage enemy positions while reducing soldiers’ exposure to direct fire.
A third, tracked unmanned vehicle was seen in social media images on Tuesday, which military bloggers described as a medium-sized unmanned vehicle for export.
The vehicle is said to weigh around 10 tonnes, with four antennas on top, a main gun, and four anti-tank Hongjian missiles.
Besides the drone and anti-drone vehicles, another two tanks were spotted at the Zhuhai air show site.
One of them was described as the newest model in the VT-4 series – China’s most successful export main battle tanks that are used by the Pakistan Army, the Royal Thai Army and the Nigerian Army.
The new tank is believed to be designated as a VT-4B and the images suggest it has had upgrades in armour protection, active protection, its weapon station and electronic equipment.
The images suggest the VT-4 has had a range of upgrades. Photo: X/WenJian0922
This year marks the 30th anniversary of the Zhuhai air show – also known as the China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition. Organisers said more than 1,100 exhibitors from nearly 50 countries and regions would participate, showcasing more than 3,000 items of equipment, around 10 per cent of which would be on public display for the first time.
By Albee Zhang

title_en: Japan’s ‘Rabbit Island’ draws tourists with fluffy bunnies and dark wartime past
content_en:
Hundreds of bunnies draw 200,000 tourists a year to Okunoshima, where the Imperial Army once ran a secret chemical weapons factory.
A tourist feeds a wild rabbit on Okunoshima Island, in Japan’s Hiroshima prefecture, in October. Photo: AFP
Stepping onto an island in western Japan, tourists squeal with joy at the sight of hundreds of fluffy rabbits, but few realise the land was once home to a secret chemical weapons factory for the country’s Imperial Army.
Okunoshima – also known as “Rabbit Island” – has a perimeter of just four kilometres (2.5 miles) but welcomes thousands of snap-happy visitors attracted by its bunny population each year.
“This was my dream,” to visit the island, 67-year-old Susan Balzer from Canada said.
“You can feed them, they come to you. We never get to really get close to them” back home, she said.
The rabbit population is thought to have grown from a small group released by a nearby junior school in the 1970s to around 500 today, aided by abundant food and a lack of predators.
But the island’s cute exterior belies a dark history.
In 1929, the former Imperial Japanese Army built a chemical weapons factory on Okunoshima in an effort to catch up with Europe, despite international bans introduced after World War I.

“A growing rabbit population does not mean the animals are happy,” Yamauchi said.
“If we want them to thrive, visitors should avoid selfishly feeding them.”

title_en: China pet ‘memorial diamond’ industry charging US$15,000 for ash gems faces scrutiny
content_en:
Industry insiders warn that video proof is easily staged or edited, and without unified standards, consumers struggle to prove fraud in disputes.
China’s pet “memorial diamond” industry is under scrutiny for charging up to 100,000 yuan (US$15,000) per carat to turn pet ashes or fur into lab-grown gems. Photo: Shutterstock/ Handout
Moving beyond traditional urns and paw-print keepsakes, some grieving pet owners in China are having their companions’ fur and ashes turned into lab-grown diamonds.
A woman in northeastern China has sparked widespread debate about the growing industry after paying 8,950 yuan (US$1,350) for a diamond ring made using her dog’s fur.
According to Jimu News, Chen Xing, from Jilin province, commissioned the ring in 2020, as her toy poodle, Baobao, entered its senior years.
The 18-karat gold ring, delivered in February 2021, features a 0.5-carat, princess-cut diamond grown using the dog’s fur.
After Baobao died in April, Chen began wearing the ring every day, saying it makes her feel as though her pet is still by her side.
According to mainland media reports, producing a pet memorial diamond typically requires at least 3g of fur.
Pet owners wear these “memorial diamonds” not just as keepsakes, but as a way to keep their late companions close after their passing. Photo: Handout
Vendors clean, dry and grind the fur or ashes to extract carbon. The carbon is then combined with other materials and subjected to high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) processes to grow a gem.
Some manufacturers even claim their stones are made entirely from carbon derived from pets.
Chen’s story reflects a booming niche market in China, where related topics have attracted more than 48 million views on social media.
One user, posting under the handle “Apple,” wrote that six months after her golden retriever died, she began wearing a diamond made in her pet’s memory alongside her wedding band every day.
“It can stay with me until I die. In a way, we are growing old together,” she wrote.
Reports indicate that at least 20 brands now offer pet memorial diamonds in China, with finished one-carat pieces typically costing 10,000 to 30,000 yuan (US$1,500-US$4,500).
At least 20 brands in China now offer pet memorial diamonds, with finished one-carat pieces typically costing 10,000 to 30,000 yuan (US$1,500-US$4,500). Photo: Handout
Luxury options cost considerably more. Swiss brand Algordanza, for example, charges from HK$101,420 (US$13,000) for a one-carat pet diamond and requires at least 11g of fur or 250g of ashes.
Domestic brands are also doing brisk business. According to Global E-businessmen, Yasheng, founded in 2021, generates several million yuan in annual sales. The company offers one-on-one videos, factory live-streams and in-person visits so clients can observe the creation process.
Ye Man, co-founder of rival brand ICEWALD, told Chao News that 80 per cent of the company’s clients are urban women aged 25 to 35 who regard pets as family and are willing to pay for that emotional bond.
Yet the industry’s rapid growth has drawn scrutiny over transparency and consumer protection.
Jewellery practitioners note that no appraisal method can confirm whether the carbon in a finished diamond actually came from a pet, leaving room for unscrupulous merchants to pass off ordinary lab-grown stones as bespoke keepsakes.
Critics say the industry exploits grieving pet owners, calling it an “IQ tax” — Chinese slang for overpriced gimmicks. Photo: Shutterstock
Industry insiders add that video documentation – the primary proof of authenticity – can easily be staged or edited. With no unified production or traceability standards, consumers may face significant hurdles in proving fraud if a dispute arises.
Public reaction, however, remains divided.
One online critic dismissed the trend as a grief-exploiting “IQ tax,” a Chinese slang term for overpriced gimmicks.
Another netizen said she preferred keeping her cat’s whiskers and fur in a pouch, calling diamonds “cold and hard.”
A third urged tolerance, noting that “every pet owner’s choice deserves respect.”
The debate highlights the scale of China’s urban pet economy, which reached 312.6 billion yuan (US$47 billion) last year, spanning 126 million dogs and cats.
By Zoey Zhang

title_en: North Korea’s Kim Jong-un visits school gear factories after apparent Trump snub
content_en:
State media shows Kim touring teaching-aid factories after the US president left Asia without securing a hoped-for meeting.
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un inspects a construction site in South Hamgyong province, North Korea, in a photo released by the Korean Central News Agency on Thursday. Photo: KCNA via Reuters
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un was seen inspecting school equipment and teaching aids, state media said on Saturday, after an apparent snub of US President Donald Trump during his Asia tour.
Trump met Kim three times during his first term and has repeatedly floated another meeting since his return to the White House, including during his Asia tour this week.
Trump left Asia late on Thursday after a landmark trilateral summit which included the Chinese and Russian presidents, without meeting Kim.
[embedded media]
The US leader suggested he was too busy to fit it in, and that he and Kim would “have that meeting at some point”.
Pyongyang has yet to comment on Trump’s remarks.
North Korea’s state media instead released images showing Kim examining teaching aids and science class equipment at factory sites.
During Friday’s visit Kim “examined the samples of school fixtures of all indices to be produced by the factory”, Pyongyang’s official Korean Central News Agency said on Saturday.
Science and education were the “clearest expression of our revolutionaries’ outlook on the future generations and the revolution”, Kim said, according to KCNA.
Trump had repeatedly raised the prospect of meeting Kim in China, saying the North Korean leader “would like to” meet him, despite Pyongyang remaining silent on the matter.
Kim was also seen visiting a ski resort and Mount Paektu earlier this week, followed by a naval university on Wednesday where he stressed the importance of maritime defence, according to state media.
Kim and Trump’s previous summits sought to curb Pyongyang’s nuclear programme but yielded no concrete deal.
Despite years of UN sanctions, North Korea has pressed ahead, enshrining its nuclear status in law and declaring its arsenal permanent and irreversible.
Analysts say Pyongyang’s closer ties with Beijing and Moscow give it less incentive to engage Washington, complicating Trump’s efforts after his party’s crushing midterm defeat.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: China’s top intelligence agency touts ‘common international security’ after summit
content_en:
The Ministry of State Security warns that no country can achieve ‘absolute security’ at the expense of others.
The Ministry of State Security commentary underlines Beijing’s messaging on security just a day after an unprecedented China-US-Russia trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Thursday. Photo: via Reuters
China’s top intelligence agency has warned that no nation can achieve “absolute security” at the expense of others, underscoring Beijing’s messaging on security just a day after Thursday’s unprecedented China-US-Russia trilateral summit.
In a commentary published on its official social account on Friday, the Ministry of State Security (MSS) framed China’s security philosophy as both a theoretical evolution of Marxism and “an urgent response to mounting geopolitical instability”.
The article, titled “Why must we persist in promoting common international security?”, reiterated Beijing’s concern that “changes unseen in a century” had ushered the world into “a new period of turbulence and transformation, with instability and uncertainty rising sharply”.
It laid out three pillars of Beijing’s security doctrine: theoretical, historical and practical.
From a theoretical perspective, the ministry said the doctrine was rooted in “Marxist world-history theory”, which holds that expanding productive forces and global exchanges bind humanity into an increasingly interconnected system, transcending isolated, closed and zero-sum confrontation.
“No country can achieve its own security in isolation from world security, nor can any country achieve security built on the insecurity of other nations,” the commentary stated, urging governments to uphold win-win principles and weigh the legitimate security concerns of others alongside their own.
[embedded media]
From a historical perspective, the agency portrayed the doctrine as the crystallisation of the Communist Party’s century-long experience. Looking back at the revolutionary war years, it said fighting colonial aggression had taught the party that “a weak nation has no security” and that “peace is hard-won”.
After the founding of the People’s Republic in 1949, Beijing pursued an independent foreign policy and opposed both bloc alliances and interference in other countries’ internal affairs, the article said. Then, after launching reform and opening up in the late 1970s, China sought to safeguard world peace through its own development, it added.
In the “new era” – a term used to describe the period since President Xi Jinping came to power at the end of 2012 – Beijing had rallied behind cooperation, innovation, the rule of law and win-win outcomes, promoting Xi’s “common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable” vision for global security, the article read.
From a practical perspective, the MSS warned that humanity faced widening deficits in peace, development, security and governance, as security challenges grew more transnational, interconnected and diverse.
“Today’s security issues have long transcended national borders,” the commentary said.
“A security weak point in any single country can invite an influx of external risks, turning that nation into an easy target for security threats. Furthermore, if security problems within a country accumulate to a certain level, they can spill over, evolving into regional or even global security challenges,” it added.
“Global threats and challenges demand a global response; no country should seek its own so-called ‘absolute security’ at the expense of the security of others.”
[embedded media]
“Only when the world is well can China be well; only when China is well can the world be even better,” the commentary concluded, calling for deeper implementation of Xi’s Global Security Initiative to build a community with a shared future for mankind characterised by universal security.
The commentary’s call to “better implement the Global Security Initiative” also highlights the central role the framework now plays in Beijing’s diplomatic and national security posture.
First unveiled by Xi at the Boao Forum in April 2022 and elaborated in a foreign ministry concept paper in February 2023, the initiative represents Beijing’s signature effort to articulate an alternative to US-led military alliances and Western security architecture.
Within Beijing’s ideological lexicon, the initiative specifically targets the “cold war mentality”, unilateral sanctions, “long-arm jurisdiction” and what Chinese officials characterise as Washington’s pursuit of “absolute security” through its alliances.
It also forms one of the four pillars of Xi’s “Four Global Initiatives” – alongside the Global Development Initiative launched in September 2021, the Global Civilisation Initiative in March 2023 and the Global Governance Initiative, which Beijing fleshed out in a dedicated white paper in June. Together, the four frameworks serve as the overarching blueprint for Beijing’s outreach to the Global South and its push to reshape international norms around a multipolar order.
By William Zheng

title_en: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ on US firms building AI data centres overseas
content_en:
US president warns America risks losing its AI lead to China if domestic backlash over power and water pushes tech giants to build abroad.
An aerial view of an Amazon Web Services data centre known as US-East-1 in Ashburn, Virginia, in October 2025. Photo: Reuters
President Donald Trump on Friday threatened “a tremendous tax” on US companies that build artificial intelligence data centres abroad, highlighting a divide between a president who sees their expansion as critical to winning the AI race and an American public that is deeply sceptical of their benefits.
Briefing reporters at the White House shortly after his return from Asia, the president said the country was ahead of China in developing what he likes to call “superintelligence”. But he warned it could fall behind if a growing political backlash puts the brakes on development of the data centres that are driving the AI boom.
“We’re not going to allow companies to build data centres in other countries,” the president said. “If they do that, they can. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.”
He contrasted his push to keep AI infrastructure in the US with the foreign production of advanced computer chips, which he said had been “very destructive to our country”.
Trump said he had not yet told his staff about his proposal to target data centre development outside the US, and it was not immediately clear how it would be enforced.
His statements emphasised the gap between Trump’s view of AI development and the views of most Americans and came less than three weeks after voter concerns about data centres contributed to a Republican wipeout in the midterm elections.
About three-quarters of US voters in this year’s election said they opposed the construction of a new data centre in their community, according to The AP Voter Poll.
In a survey taken over the summer, about six in 10 Americans said they supported limiting the number of new data centres that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans, according to the poll by Associated Press-NORC Centre for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago.
The same survey found that a majority of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centres on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.
A sign calling for a ban on data centres stands outside a home near Meta’s Prometheus Campus AI supercluster project in New Albany, Ohio, on November 1, 2026. Photo: Getty Images via AFP
With Democrats winning large majorities in both houses of Congress, a tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data centre developers is expected to follow, even if Trump – perhaps the industry’s biggest champion – stalls any federal crackdown.
He suggested that data centre concerns could be addressed through community negotiations with the tech companies seeking to build them. Tax breaks, reduced utility bills, money for teachers and direct payments to local residents all could be part of the talks.
“Make the deal,” Trump said. “They have plenty of money. Take it.”
The development of artificial intelligence is an important growth factor for data centres, but cloud computing services remain the dominant use of data centres in the US, industry officials say.
With host communities across the US turning against the gargantuan data centres, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets and shower more money on communities willing to allow the server warehouses.
Besides ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta Platforms said in interviews they were trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build.
Companies also are making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centres will boost local property values – all while maintaining that AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its sceptics.
“We want them to build it here,” Trump said.
Many of the tech giants already have global footprints. Google has data centres in Asia and Europe.
